lesson.subtitle: Lesson 6 -- No Room at the Hotel
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Veridiana Sterman Petrilli | Lesson 6 -- No Room at the Hotel

listenings.text: I answer consumer complaints for a living, and people always ask me the same thing. When should I ask for a supervisor? My answer is: later than you think, and earlier than never. The person at the desk has a list of things they are allowed to authorise, and that list is short. It is not that they do not want to help you. They physically cannot. So the first question is not can I speak to a manager. The first question is: what are you able to offer me yourself? If the answer covers your problem, you are finished in two minutes. If it does not, then you say it plainly: if that is everything you can authorise, could you ask a supervisor? That sentence is not aggressive. It tells the person in front of you that you understand their limit, and it moves the case up without making an enemy. And one more thing, which is the piece almost nobody does. Ask for it in writing. Not because you plan to go to court, but because a company that has written something down remembers it.

I was a duty supervisor at an airport for nine years, so let me tell you what actually happened on my side of the desk. When a passenger came to me, I already knew the problem. What I did not know was what would satisfy them, and that is the thing they almost never said. Somebody would talk for four minutes about how long they had waited, and I still had no idea what I was supposed to do. The passengers who got the most were the ones who finished with a sentence like this: if you can get us on the morning flight, we will take it; if you cannot, we will need a hotel and dinner tonight. Two options, both reasonable, and now I am choosing instead of guessing. Unless the request was impossible, I gave them one of the two, and I did it fast, because there were forty people behind them. And the passenger who only said this is unacceptable got nothing, every single time, because there was nothing for me to say yes to.

reading.rtitle: The Sentence That Moves a Desk
paras: Every company that sells rooms, seats or tickets has the same problem: it promises something it cannot always deliver. The room is sold, the flight is full, the tour is cancelled. What happens next is not decided by who is angriest. It is decided by what the person behind the desk is allowed to authorise, and by whether the customer in front of them has said anything that can be acted on.

The first thing to understand is availability. A desk agent can only give you what exists. If there is no room in the building, no amount of explaining will produce one. What the agent does have is a short list: an alternative hotel, a taxi, a meal, a refund of part of the price, sometimes a voucher for a future stay. The list is short, it is written down somewhere, and it is not the same as what a supervisor can authorise.

The second thing is the shape of what you say. Compare two customers. The first one says this is unacceptable, and repeats it. There is nothing in that sentence for the agent to say yes to. The second one says: if you can move us to another hotel tonight, we will take it; unless you can cover the taxi as well, we will need something for dinner. Two options, both reasonable, both possible, and a deadline that is tonight. The agent is now choosing, not guessing.

The third thing is what you do when the list runs out. Do not open with a demand for a manager. Ask what the agent can authorise themselves, and only if that does not cover the problem, say the sentence that escalates without making an enemy: if that is everything you can authorise, could you ask a supervisor? And whatever you agree, ask for it in writing. A company that has written something down remembers it, and the e-mail costs the agent thirty seconds. Most disagreements settle right there, at the desk, in under five minutes.
reading.source: Written for this lesson, from how consumer advisers and airport duty supervisors describe the same conversation.

choices: To argue that hotels and airlines should stop selling more than they have.
To show what the person behind the desk can actually do, and how to say something they can act on.
To explain how to take a company to court after a bad trip.

items.situation: Offer the desk two options for tonight, in one sentence.
tips: If you can move us to another hotel tonight, we will take it; if you cannot, we will need dinner and a taxi.
If + present, then will + bare verb. Never if we will move us.

items.situation: Say what you will do if they do not cover the taxi, using unless.
tips: Unless you cover the taxi, we will have to pay for it ourselves.
Unless already means if not, so it never takes a second not.

items.situation: Ask for a supervisor without blaming the person in front of you.
tips: If that is everything you can authorise, could you ask a supervisor?
The condition does the work, so the request stays polite.

items.situation: Ask for the agreement in writing, and give a reason.
tips: Could you send that to me in an e-mail? If I have it in writing, nobody has to remember it tomorrow.
One short reason turns a demand into something easy to say yes to.

items.situation: Set a deadline that is not aggressive.
tips: If we do not hear anything by six, we will book somewhere ourselves.
A deadline is a fact about you, not a threat about them.

items.situation: Now use the same shape for a real problem in your own practice, with a patient.
tips: If you cannot come on Thursday, we will move you to the following week.
Same structure, different room: if + present, will + bare verb.
